history.heading: Polynesian heartland
paragraphs: French Polynesia comprises 118 islands and atolls in five archipelagos, including the Society Islands (with Tahiti and Bora Bora), the Marquesas and the Tuamotus, spread over an area of ocean as large as Western Europe. Polynesians settled the islands around 1,000 years ago, and they were a centre from which voyagers reached Hawaii and New Zealand. The marae of Taputapuātea on Raiatea, a sacred site, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
European explorers, including Samuel Wallis, Louis-Antoine de Bougainville and James Cook, arrived in the 18th century. The mutiny on the Bounty in 1789 followed a stay in Tahiti.

history.heading: French rule
paragraphs: The Pomare dynasty unified Tahiti with the help of missionaries. France established a protectorate in 1842 and annexed the islands in 1880. The painter Paul Gauguin lived and worked there in the 1890s.

From 1966 to 1996, France conducted 193 nuclear tests at Moruroa and Fangataufa atolls, which caused health and environmental damage and protests; France has acknowledged their impact and offers compensation to victims.

culture.heading: Polynesian culture
paragraphs: French is official, and Tahitian and other Polynesian languages are widely spoken. Most people are Christian, mainly Protestant and Catholic. Traditional culture, including tattooing (tatau), outrigger canoe racing (va'a) and dance ('ori Tahiti), has been revived.
The Heiva festival each July celebrates Polynesian dance, music and sports. Poisson cru, raw fish in lime and coconut milk, is the national dish.

politics.heading: Overseas collectivity
paragraphs: French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France with a high degree of autonomy, its own president, government and assembly, while France handles defence, justice, security and foreign affairs. Politics is divided between parties favouring autonomy within France and those seeking independence; the UN lists it as a non-self-governing territory.

economy.heading: Tourism and pearls
paragraphs: Tourism is the main industry, with luxury overwater bungalows in Bora Bora and Moorea. Tahitian black pearls are the leading export. French government spending, fishing and agriculture (copra, vanilla and noni) are also important.
The currency is the CFP franc, pegged to the euro.
